passages.text: When I said, “I would like to meet someone among those who had seen him,” they immediately led me away, saying, “There is someone here who has not only become personally acquainted with him but is also from the land there—a Hebrew man named Barnabas. He also says that he is one of his disciples, and, sitting somewhere around here, he readily tells those who wish to hear the words of that man’s promise.” So I went along with them. When I arrived, I stood with the crowd that was present, listening to his words, and I realized that he was speaking the truth, not by dialectical skill, but was setting out without guile and without preparation both what he had heard and what he had seen the Son of God who had appeared do and say. He also supplied, from the very crowd then present, many witnesses for both the wonders and the words he was recounting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I would like to meet someone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperfect ἤθελον can express a polite or tentative desire; “I wanted to meet” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who has not only become personally acquainted with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω with a person can mean visiting or gaining firsthand acquaintance, not merely collecting information. “Who has visited him” or “who has investigated him” are possible but less responsive to Clement’s request to meet an eyewitness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the words of that man’s promise
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόσχεσις denotes a promise or undertaking. The demonstrative is retained rather than replaced with a named referent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: without guile and without preparation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both Barnabas’s lack of deceit or artifice and the extemporaneous character of his presentation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Son of God who had appeared
lexical_decisions.rationale: φανέντα describes the Son as having appeared or become manifest; the wording does not itself specify how that appearance is to be understood.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ λεγομένων θαυμασίων τε καὶ λόγων
lexical_decisions.chosen: for both the wonders and the words he was recounting
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive identifies what the witnesses attest. αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to Barnabas as the one recounting them, though the words and wonders themselves concern the appeared Son.

source_issues.issue: This is a non-Attic or later perfect form of ὁράω rather than the classical-looking ἑωρακότων. The same passage later prints ἑόρακεν, supporting an orthographic pattern rather than an unreadable source. The meaning is secure, and the printed form is not emended in the translation.

passages.text: But because the crowds were favorably disposed toward what was being said without guile, the philosophers who came from a worldly education began laughing at him and jeering at him, making jokes and deriding him with immeasurable insolence, as though they were wielding syllogisms as mighty weapons. He, however, thrust aside their nonsense and did not join in their crafty questioning; instead, undaunted, he continued speaking without stopping. Once someone asked him why a gnat came into being and, though extremely small, has six feet and also wings, whereas the elephant, the largest of animals, though wingless, has only four feet. After the question, he took up the discourse that had been interrupted. As his answer to the question, he resumed the discourse that had been before him from the beginning, using only the following preface after each interruption: “We have been commanded only to tell you the words and marvelous deeds of the one who sent us. Instead of a logical demonstration, we offer you many witnesses from among you who are present, whose faces I remember as living images and sufficient testimonies. From this point it is within your power to yield or to disobey. But I will not cease telling you what benefits you, because silence is loss to me, while disobedience is harm to you. I could also supply demonstrations in answer to your groundless challenges, if you were asking with love for truth. But it is not timely now to tell you, who are ignorant of the God of all things, the reason for the differing creation of the gnat and the elephant.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὰ ἀπανούργως λεγόμενα· ἡδέως οἱ ὄχλοι διετίθεντο
lexical_decisions.chosen: the crowds were favorably disposed toward what was being said without guile
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἡδέως διετίθεντο describes a favorable or pleased response, while ἀπανούργως emphasizes the absence of craftiness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ συνέτρεχεν αὐτῶν τῇ πανούργῳ πεύσει
lexical_decisions.chosen: did not join in their crafty questioning
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal image is that he did not “run together with” their questioning. The English expresses his refusal to follow them into their contrived line of inquiry.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he took up the discourse that had been interrupted
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐμποδίζω here describes the discourse as impeded by the question, and ἀναλαμβάνω marks its resumption.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς πρὸς τὴν πεῦσιν ἀποκρινάμενος τὸν αὐτῷ ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς προκείμενον ἀνελάμβανεν λόγον
lexical_decisions.chosen: As his answer to the question, he resumed the discourse that had been before him from the beginning
lexical_decisions.rationale: The main rendering treats his resumption of the discourse as his response to the question, fitting the following statement that he repeatedly used the same preface when interrupted. Because ὡς with the aorist participle may instead mark assumed posture or manner, the clause can also be rendered, “As though he had answered the question, he resumed the discourse that had been before him from the beginning.” On that reading, the narrator does not present the resumed discourse straightforwardly as an answer, but describes Barnabas as proceeding as one who had answered.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὧν ἐγὼ τὰ εἴδη μέμνημαι ὡς ἐμψύχους εἰκόνας ἱκανὰς μαρτυρίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose faces I remember as living images and sufficient testimonies
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἴδη can mean forms, appearances, or faces. “Faces” suits remembered eyewitnesses; “whose forms I remember” remains possible. The appositional language treats those remembered appearances as living images and adequate testimony.

lexical_decisions.chosen: your groundless challenges
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰκαῖος can describe what is random, purposeless, or without sound basis, while προβλήματα are questions or challenges put forward. “Your random questions” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you, who are ignorant of the God of all things
lexical_decisions.rationale: τῶν ὅλων belongs with θεόν and identifies God as God of the totality, not merely as a god unknown in some limited respect.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ δὲ πρὸς τὰ ἀπανούργως λεγόμενα· ἡδέως οἱ ὄχλοι διετίθεντο
source_issues.issue: The printed middle point after λεγόμενα interrupts the ἐπειδή clause even though ἡδέως οἱ ὄχλοι διετίθεντο supplies its finite verb. This appears to be editorial punctuation rather than missing wording, and the translation construes the clause continuously.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἐπειδὴ δὲ πρὸς τὰ ἀπανούργως λεγόμενα ἡδέως οἱ ὄχλοι διετίθεντο,

passages.text: As he was saying these things, they let loose disorderly laughter as though by common agreement, trying to silence him and leave him at a loss, as though he were some raving barbarian. When I saw this, I was seized—I do not know how—with zeal and pious indignation. I could no longer endure remaining silent, but cried out boldly, saying: “With good reason God has made his will incomprehensible to you, foreseeing that you were unworthy, as is now evident from the very things by which he fully convinces those who possess discerning minds. For heralds of his will have now been sent out, not professing grammatical art, but displaying his will in simple and guileless words, so that absolutely anyone, upon hearing, understands what is being said, and not with some grudging polish that is unwilling to make itself available to everyone. Yet here you are: besides not understanding what benefits you, you laugh, to your own harm, at the truth that has lived as a citizen among barbarians—to your condemnation. Though it has now visited even you, you do not wish to receive it as a guest, because of your wanton conduct and the plainness of its words, so that you may not be exposed as people who are lovers of words to no purpose and not philosophers who love truth. How long, then, will you keep learning to talk, you who do not know how to speak well? For many utterances from you are not worth one word. What, then, will your Greek multitude say, once it has become one soul, if there is indeed to be a judgment, as this man says? ‘Why, God, did you not proclaim your will to us?’ Will you not surely hear—if indeed you are deemed worthy of an answer—the following? ‘I knew, before the foundation of the world, every choice that would be made, and secretly went beforehand to meet each person according to what that person deserved. But wishing to give those who have taken refuge with me full assurance of this very fact—that it is so, and why I did not allow my will to be proclaimed publicly from the beginning, starting with earlier generations—I have now, near the end of life, sent heralds of my counsel. They are laughed at and, while being insulted, are mocked by people who wish to receive no benefit and who have forcefully rejected my friendship. Oh, the magnitude of the injustice! Heralds risk being murdered, and this at the hands of men who are being called to salvation!’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: as though he were some raving barbarian
lexical_decisions.rationale: δαιμονάω can suggest being possessed or behaving madly. “Raving” preserves the hostile characterization without deciding whether the mockers meant literal possession.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ζήλῳ οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅπως ληφθεὶς εὐσεβεῖ θυμῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: seized—I do not know how—with zeal and pious indignation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two datival expressions describe Clement’s impelling zeal and religiously framed passion or anger. θυμός could also be rendered “ardor” or “anger.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἐξ ὧν νῦν τοὺς κριτικὸν νοῦν ἔχοντας πληροφορῶν φαίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: as is now evident from the very things by which he fully convinces those who possess discerning minds
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering takes φαίνεται impersonally in English and treats ἐξ ὧν as the evidentiary basis by which God convinces discerning people. Alternatively, the phrase may mean that God’s present convincing of discerning people is itself what makes the hearers’ unworthiness apparent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not professing grammatical art
lexical_decisions.rationale: γραμματικὴ τέχνη refers to educated literary or grammatical expertise. The relatively literal wording preserves the contrast with the heralds’ simple speech.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ μετὰ ξέσεώς τινος φθονερᾶς, παρέχειν πᾶσιν ἑαυτὴν μὴ βουλομένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: not with some grudging polish that is unwilling to make itself available to everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξέσις is literally a scraping or polishing and here depicts refined rhetorical finish. The feminine participle most directly agrees with ξέσεως, personifying such refinement as grudgingly inaccessible; it could alternatively be understood more broadly of an elitist mode of presentation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν καταδίκην ἐν βαρβάροις πολιτευσαμένην ἀλήθειαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the truth that has lived as a citizen among barbarians—to your condemnation
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεύομαι carries civic imagery: truth has conducted its life or held citizenship among those the Greeks call barbarians. The following ξενίσαι continues the contrasting guest imagery.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰκῇ φιλόλογοί ἐστε καὶ οὐ φιλαληθεῖς φιλόσοφοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: you are lovers of words to no purpose and not philosophers who love truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording preserves the author’s contrast and wordplay between φιλόλογοι, φιλαληθεῖς, and φιλόσοφοι. εἰκῇ marks their devotion to words as vain or purposeless.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Will you not surely hear
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this rhetorical question πάντως is taken affirmatively as “surely” or “certainly.” In a declarative setting οὐ πάντως could instead mean “not altogether” or “not necessarily,” but that reading fits the present question poorly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάσας τὰς ἐσομένας πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου εἰδὼς προαιρέσεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: I knew, before the foundation of the world, every choice that would be made
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαίρεσις can denote a choice, purpose, or moral disposition. “Choice” preserves the emphasis on acts or orientations of volition without adding a developed theory of free will.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦτο δὲ αὐτὸ ὅτι οὕτως ἔχει βουληθεὶς τοὺς προσπεφευγότας μοι πληροφορήσαι διὰ τί
lexical_decisions.chosen: wishing to give those who have taken refuge with me full assurance of this very fact—that it is so, and why
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering treats ὅτι οὕτως ἔχει and the following διὰ τί clause as coordinated content of πληροφορήσαι. It is also possible to construe the wording more tightly as assurance precisely about why matters stand this way.

lexical_decisions.chosen: near the end of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: βίος literally denotes life or its course. In this universal historical context it may refer more broadly to the close of the present course of worldly life, but “age” or “world” is not explicitly written.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who have forcefully rejected my friendship
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραιτέομαι means declining, refusing, or rejecting, and ἐπιτεταμένως gives the refusal an emphatic or strenuous character.

passages.text: “‘This injustice being committed against my heralds would have been committed against everyone from the beginning, if the unworthy had been called to salvation from the beginning. For what they now do unjustly serves as a defense of my just providence: I rightly did not wish, from the beginning, to expose publicly to abuse, and to no benefit, the message worthy of honor. Instead, I resolved that it should be kept unspoken as something precious—not withheld from those who were worthy from the beginning, for I did share it with them, but from these people and others like them, who, as you see, are unworthy, who hate me and do not wish to love themselves.’ And now, at any rate, stop laughing at this man. Question me about his proclamation, or let anyone who wishes answer me when I question him. Do not bark like wanton dogs, shutting the ears of those who wish to be saved with disorderly noise. You unjust people, hateful to God and turning the reasoning that saves aside into unbelief, how can you obtain pardon when you insult the man who offers to tell you about God’s divine nature—and that too a man whom you ought to have welcomed because of his good intention toward you, even if he said nothing true?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the message worthy of honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος here is the proclaimed teaching or message rather than merely an individual word. “The discourse worthy of honor” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to expose publicly to abuse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal construction is to “place” the message publicly into insult or outrage. “Expose publicly to abuse” conveys both the placement and its intended result.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it should be kept unspoken as something precious
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive σιγᾶσθαι means that the message is to be kept silent or left unspoken, while τίμιον can mean precious, highly valued, or honorable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἀξίων (οἷς καὶ μετέδωκα), ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ τούτων καὶ τῶν τοιούτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: not withheld from those who were worthy from the beginning, for I did share it with them, but from these people and others like them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated ἀπό depends on the idea of being kept unspoken from particular groups. “Withheld” makes that relation idiomatic without supplying any missing content.

lexical_decisions.chosen: about his proclamation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπάγγελμα can mean a declaration, profession, undertaking, claim, or promise. Here it denotes what Barnabas publicly professes or proclaims; “about his claim” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: bark like wanton dogs
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀσελγής may mean wanton, shameless, insolent, or undisciplined. “Wanton” preserves the severity of the insult without narrowing it to sexual misconduct.

lexical_decisions.chosen: hateful to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound most naturally has a passive sense, “hated by” or “hateful to God,” and commonly characterizes the impious. “God-hating” is lexically possible if the compound is taken actively.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν σώζοντα λογισμὸν εἰς ἀπιστίαν ἀπασχολοῦντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: turning the reasoning that saves aside into unbelief
lexical_decisions.rationale: λογισμός is reasoning, reflection, or the rational faculty, and ἀπασχολέω describes diverting or preoccupying it. The phrase depicts their noise as redirecting potentially saving thought toward unbelief.

lexical_decisions.chosen: God’s divine nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: θειότης denotes divinity or divine nature. The rendering retains the source’s explicit genitive “of God” rather than replacing it with a different theological formulation.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ νῦν γε παρέντες· γελᾶν τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον ἐμοῦ πρὸς τὸ τούτου ἐπάγγελμα πυνθάνεσθε
source_issues.issue: The printed middle point after παρέντες separates the participle from the infinitive γελᾶν, although παρέντες γελᾶν gives the defensible sense “stop laughing.” The translation treats the punctuation as editorial and construes ἐμοῦ with πυνθάνεσθε, “question me.” No wording is supplied or removed.
source_issues.proposed_reading: καὶ νῦν γε, παρέντες γελᾶν τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον, ἐμοῦ πρὸς τὸ τούτου ἐπάγγελμα πυνθάνεσθε
